subject: GOWANS et al. (1964)
object: GOWANS et al. (1964) studied familial factors in rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: BURCH et al. (1964)
object: BURCH et al. (1964) reported family and genetic studies of rheumatoid arthritis and rheumatoid factor in Blackfeet Indians.

subject: Stastny and Fink (1979)
object: Stastny and Fink (1979) performed HLA-D typing in 126 patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. HLA-DW4, the antigen associated with adult rheumatoid arthritis in earlier studies, was significantly less frequent in children with arthritis than in normal controls (P less than 0.04). In contrast, HLA-DW7 (P less than 0.03) and HLA-DW8 (P less than 0.01) were increased in the children. The authors concluded that adult rheumatoid arthritis and arthritis of childhood differ fundamentally.

subject: Stastny and Fink (1979)
object: Stastny and Fink (1979) found that TMo, an HLA-D antigen detected with homozygous typing cells from a child with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, was related to the cross-reactive specificities HLA-DW7 and DW11. TMo was present in 46% of patients with persistent pauciarticular arthritis of childhood, compared with 1% of normal controls, giving a relative risk of 67.7 (P less than 0.0001). The authors suggested that childhood arthritis includes a clinically distinguishable group characterized by TMo.

subject: Gregersen et al. (1987)
object: Gregersen et al. (1987) proposed the shared epitope hypothesis as an approach to understanding the molecular genetics of susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Weyand et al. (1992)
object: Weyand et al. (1992) stratified 81 patients with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis by disease manifestations and typed HLA-DRB1 alleles by PCR and oligonucleotide hybridization, confirming homozygosity by locus-specific cDNA amplification and sequencing. They found that rheumatoid nodules were highly associated with heterozygosity for 2 disease-associated HLA-DRB1 alleles, whereas homozygosity for HLA-DRB1*0401 was characteristic of RA patients with major organ involvement.

subject: HLA-DRB1 HLA-DRB1*0401
object: HLA-DRB1

subject: Weyand et al. (1992)
object: Weyand et al. (1992) suggested that the disease-associated sequence motif in the third hypervariable region of HLA-DRB1 plays a role in determining RA severity, and that the codominant function of HLA-DRB1 alleles implies that HLA-DR function in thymic selection might be important in RA pathogenesis.

subject: Bell et al. (1992)
object: Bell et al. (1992) described deficiency of the monocyte ectoenzyme non-specific esterase in 4 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The deficiency followed a heredofamilial pattern. They found no association of the deficiency with HLA status or with rheumatoid factor seropositivity.

subject: Hasstedt et al. (1994)
object: Hasstedt et al. (1994) studied 28 pedigrees ascertained through pairs of first-degree relatives with rheumatoid arthritis, in which RA was confirmed in 77 members and absence of disease verified in 261 members, all serologically typed for HLA. Likelihood analysis assuming tight linkage to HLA supported an HLA-linked RA susceptibility locus with a susceptibility allele frequency of 2.16% and lifetime penetrance of 41% in male and 48% in female homozygotes; inheritance was recessive in males and nearly recessive in females.

subject: Hasstedt et al. (1994)
object: Hasstedt et al. (1994) estimated that the HLA-linked RA susceptibility locus accounts for approximately one-half of familial RA but only about one-fifth of RA in the population, suggesting that other genes may account for the remaining familial RA and that a large portion of cases may occur sporadically. The analysis attributed 78% of the variance within genotypes to genetic or environmental effects shared by siblings.

subject: Lynn et al. (1995)
object: Lynn et al. (1995) did family studies and segregation analyses of rheumatoid arthritis based on consecutive patients ascertained without regard to family history, including first-degree relatives from 135 simplex and 30 multiplex families. A highly penetrant recessive major gene with a mutant allele frequency of 0.005 was identified as the most parsimonious genetic risk factor.

subject: Lynn et al. (1995)
object: Lynn et al. (1995) found significant heterogeneity in RA risk by proband gender but not by proband age at onset. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that both proband gender and age at onset were risk factors, with proband gender the more important determinant; relatives of male probands had the greatest cumulative risk. Log-linear modeling found proband gender, familiality (multiplex or simplex), and their interaction adequate to define risk in families, and the authors concluded that the pattern of risk and its inheritance is heterogeneous.

subject: Lynn et al. (1995)
object: Lynn et al. (1995) suggested that families with an excess of affected males with young age at onset may be the most informative for identifying the putative recessive gene and its modifiers.

subject: Nabozny et al. (1996)
object: Nabozny et al. (1996) generated transgenic mice expressing the HLA-DQA1*0301 and DQB1*0302 genes from a rheumatoid arthritis-predisposing haplotype (DQ8/DR4Dw4) on a mouse class II-deficient H-2Ab0 background, and found that the HLA-DQ8+,H-2Ab0 mice expressed the DQ8 molecule well with no detectable surface expression of endogenous murine class II molecules and selected CD4+ T cells with a normal V beta T cell receptor repertoire.

subject: Nabozny et al. (1996)
object: Nabozny et al. (1996) reported that immunization of HLA-DQ8+,H-2Ab0 transgenic mice with bovine type II collagen induced a strong antibody response cross-reactive with homologous mouse type II collagen and in vitro proliferative responses that were blocked by antibodies specific for HLA-DQ and mouse CD4, and that a severe polyarthritis developed in a majority of the mice, indistinguishable from the disease in arthritis-susceptible B10.T(6R) (H-2Aq) controls, whereas HLA-DQ8-negative,H-2Ab0 full sibs generated no collagen antibody and were completely resistant to arthritis.

subject: Nabozny et al. (1996)
object: Nabozny et al. (1996) concluded that their results strongly suggested that HLA-DQ8 molecules contribute to genetic susceptibility to arthritis and established a novel animal model for the study of human arthritis.

subject: Nabozny et al. (1996)
object: Nabozny et al. (1996) noted that genetic studies had indicated that susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis (RA) maps to the HLA-DR locus of the major histocompatibility complex, and that strong linkage disequilibrium between certain HLA-DQ genes and RA-associated HLA-DR genes suggested that HLA-DQ molecules may also play a role in RA susceptibility.

subject: Vyse and Todd (1996)
object: Vyse and Todd (1996) reviewed the genetic analysis of autoimmune disease.

subject: Nanki et al. (1996)
object: Nanki et al. (1996) used a PCR-ELISA method to study T cell receptor BJ gene expression in peripheral T lymphocytes from 12 pairs of monozygotic twins, including 6 pairs discordant for rheumatoid arthritis, and 5 normal individuals, focusing on the TCRBV5, 13, and 17 families reported to be increased in RA. BJ gene repertoires of monozygotic twins were more similar than those of unrelated individuals, and RA inflammation did not induce specific changes in the genetically determined pattern of BJ expression. The authors concluded that the frequency of expression of particular TCRBV-TCRBJ recombinants is genetically controlled and maintained despite chronic inflammatory disease.

subject: Vingsbo et al. (1996)
object: Vingsbo et al. (1996) presented pristane-induced arthritis in rats as a novel animal model for rheumatoid arthritis; 2 weeks after a single intradermal injection of 150 microliters of the synthetic adjuvant oil pristane, rats developed severe and chronic arthritis in which the inflammation was restricted to the joints and involved pannus formation, MHC class II expression, and T-lymphocyte infiltration.

subject: Vingsbo et al. (1996)
object: Vingsbo et al. (1996) found that both the initial development and the chronic stage of pristane-induced arthritis in rats were ameliorated by treatment with antibodies to the alpha-beta T-cell receptor, showing that the disease is T cell dependent.

subject: Vingsbo et al. (1996)
object: In the rat pristane-induced arthritis model, Vingsbo et al. (1996) observed increased serum levels of interleukin after pristane injection but not during the chronic stage of arthritis, and joint erosions were accompanied by elevated serum levels of cartilage oligomeric matrix protein.

subject: Vingsbo et al. (1996)
object: Comparing MHC congenic LEW rat strains, Vingsbo et al. (1996) showed that the severity and chronicity of pristane-induced arthritis varied among the different MHC haplotypes, with rats of the RT1f haplotype showing significantly higher susceptibility; a strong influence of non-MHC genes was also suggested by the variability of arthritis susceptibility among different strains sharing the same MHC haplotype, the most susceptible background being DA and the least susceptible E3.

subject: Vingsbo et al. (1996)
object: Vingsbo et al. (1996) concluded that arthritis induced with a well defined nonimmunogenic adjuvant, with a disease course closely resembling that of rheumatoid arthritis, makes a suitable animal model for future studies of the pathology and genetics of rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Bradley et al. (1997)
object: Bradley et al. (1997) produced mice transgenic for HLA-DQ6, an allele associated with a nonsusceptible haplotype, and found that they were resistant to collagen-induced arthritis (CIA). The authors had previously shown that mice transgenic for HLA-DQ8, an RA-associated allele, developed severe arthritis after immunization with type II collagen.

subject: Bradley et al. (1997)
object: Bradley et al. (1997) found that double-transgenic mice expressing both HLA-DQ6 and HLA-DQ8 developed moderate collagen-induced arthritis, whereas DQ8 transgenic mice developed severe arthritis. The authors compared this to RA patients who carry both susceptible and nonsusceptible HLA haplotypes and concluded that the results support a role for HLA-DQ polymorphism in human RA.

subject: Cornélis et al. (1998)
object: Cornélis et al. (1998) carried out a genome scan in 114 European Caucasian RA sib pairs from 97 nuclear families. Linkage was significant only for HLA (P < 2.5 x 10(-5)). It was nominal (P < 0.05) for 19 markers in 14 other regions, 4 of which possibly overlap with loci implicated in IDDM (IDDM6, IDDM9, IDDM13, and DXS998).

subject: Cornélis et al. (1998)
object: Cornélis et al. (1998) examined the 18q22-q23 candidate region (D18S68-D18S61-D18S469) and the 3q13 candidate region (D3S1267) in a further 194 RA sib pairs from 164 nuclear families. Only the chromosome 3 region showed significantly extended support for linkage (P = 0.002). Across all 261 families the evidence for linkage was P = 0.001, and the authors suggested that this putative RA locus interacts with HLA. They estimated that the locus could account for 16% of the genetic component of RA and proposed the genes encoding CD80 and CD86 as candidates.

subject: Cornélis et al. (1998)
object: Cornélis et al. (1998) noted that familial aggregation (lambda-s = 5), twin studies, and segregation analysis suggest a genetic component to RA. HLA, the only known susceptibility locus, had been estimated to account for one-third of this component.

subject: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998)
object: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) studied pristane-induced arthritis (PIA) in rats, a model of RA in which a single subcutaneous injection of the non-immunogenic oil pristane into susceptible DA rats induces arthritis restricted to peripheral joints with a chronic relapsing course. They crossed susceptible DA rats with resistant E3 rats; F1 rats developed chronic PIA, indicating dominant genes, but with delayed onset and reduced severity, suggesting recessive and/or additive genes. As in RA, joint involvement was predominantly symmetric, and females were more susceptible than males.

subject: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998)
object: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) performed a genome screen of 153 (E3xDA) F2 rats with 330 informative microsatellites and found that different arthritis phenotypes were associated with different loci: Pia3 on chromosome 6 and Pia2 on chromosome 4 (significant only in females) controlled arthritis onset; Pia4 on chromosome 12 controlled severity and joint erosion, with linkage also to serum cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) levels; and Pia5 (chromosome 4, in males) and Pia6 (chromosome 14) controlled chronicity. Loci controlling onset did not influence progression, and chronicity loci were not associated with onset or severity.

subject: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998)
object: Vingsbo-Lundberg et al. (1998) noted that the chronicity locus Pia5 lies near the previously described Cia3 collagen-induced arthritis locus and the Lyp/Iddm1 locus associated with lymphopenia, diabetes, and thyroiditis in the BB rat, which they suggested may indicate a common susceptibility gene for several autoimmune diseases.

subject: Cox et al. (1999)
object: Cox et al. (1999) used the combined sib-TDT and TDT, together with parametric and nonparametric linkage methods, to study the interleukin-1 (IL-1) gene cluster on chromosome 2q13 in RA families. Several tightly linked IL-1 cluster markers gave suggestive evidence for linkage in the combined TDT in families where affected sibs did not share 2 HLA-DRB1 alleles identical by descent, and the evidence was significant in patients with severe, erosive disease. Nonparametric linkage analysis showed no evidence of linkage, but parametric analysis gave weak evidence when marker-trait disequilibrium was included. The authors concluded that the data provided preliminary evidence for linkage of IL-1 cluster genes to RA and suggested a possible role for this region in severe erosive disease.

subject: Müller-Ladner et al. (2000)
object: Müller-Ladner et al. (2000) used in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry to study IL-4 STAT and its related kinase Jak-1 in frozen synovial sections from patients with short-term (less than 1 year) and long-term (more than 2 years) rheumatoid arthritis. IL-4 STAT mRNA was found in synovium at both disease stages, most intensely in follicular inflammatory infiltrates, and both fibroblasts and macrophages of the synovial lining expressed it. Synoviocytes expressed IL-4 STAT and Jak-1 protein, IL-4 stimulation up-regulated them, and phosphorylation of IL-4 STAT showed that it was activated. The authors concluded that IL-4 STAT-dependent pathways operate in early and late RA and presumably contribute to inhibitory immune mechanisms in the synovium.

subject: Zanelli et al. (2001)
object: Zanelli et al. (2001) analyzed allele distributions of 6 microsatellites in the HLA region (D6S1014, D6S273, TNFalpha, MIB, C1-2-5, and C1-3-2) in 132 RA patients and 254 controls, defining 19 microsatellite clusters corresponding to ancestral haplotypes. The MIB*350 allele, part of a cluster often associated with DQB1*0201-DRB1*0301, was found to be an RA-predisposing factor independent of DRB1*0301 and of the RA-predisposing haplotypes DQB1*03-DRB1*04 and DQB1*0501-DRB1*01. The authors concluded that the telomeric part of the HLA region contains a locus conferring predisposition to RA independently of HLA class II.

subject: Ota et al. (2001)
object: Ota et al. (2001) tested 18 microsatellite markers spanning the 3.6-Mb HLA region, from HSET at the centromeric end to P5-15 at the telomeric end, for association with rheumatoid arthritis. Allele association analysis placed one RA susceptibility gene at HLA-DRB1, as expected. It also suggested a second susceptibility gene in the HLA class III region, within a 70-kb interval just telomeric of the TNF gene cluster (TNFA and LTA), between the microsatellites TNFa and C1-2-A.

subject: Ota et al. (2001)
object: Ota et al. (2001) noted that four expressed genes had so far been identified in the critical 70-kb segment: NFKBIL1, ATP6G, BAT1 and MICB, all candidate RA susceptibility genes. The authors stated that their results excluded TNFA (TNF-alpha), previously suggested as a strong candidate for RA in the class III region.

subject: Allcock et al. (2001)
object: Allcock et al. (2001) described haplotypic single nucleotide polymorphisms in IKBL, a gene in the central MHC and a potential regulator of NF-kappaB function.

subject: Holm et al. (2001)
object: Holm et al. (2001) produced a rat strain congenic for Oia3, a quantitative trait locus originally identified as an oil-induced arthritis (OIA) QTL in arthritis-prone DA rats, by transferring a 46-cM telomeric region of chromosome 10 encompassing Oia3 from DA rats into MHC-identical but minimally arthritis-susceptible LEW.1AV1 rats by selective breeding; they noted that, although several QTLs regulating risk of experimental arthritis had been identified by genome-wide linkage analyses, only the MHC had thus far been reported to transfer arthritis susceptibility in congenic animals.

subject: Holm et al. (2001)
object: Holm et al. (2001) provoked arthritis in Oia3-congenic rats by intradermal injection of different adjuvant oils; squalene, an endogenous cholesterol precursor that is approved for vaccinations in humans and has been implicated in Gulf War syndrome, induced T cell infiltration into joints and macroscopic arthritis in Oia3-congenic and DA rats, whereas LEW.1AV1 rats were almost resistant. Arthritis onset approximately 14 days post-injection coincided with arrested body-weight gain and increased plasma levels of the inflammation markers fibrinogen and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein, and congenic rats showed intermediate phenotypes compared with the 2 parental strains.

subject: Holm et al. (2001)
object: Holm et al. (2001) observed a female preponderance of squalene-induced arthritis in Oia3-congenic rats, similar to rheumatoid arthritis in humans, and by constructing recombinant rat strains mapped a susceptibility gene or genes in females to a telomeric 4-19 cM subregion of Oia3; they concluded that the experimental system allowed transformation of multifactorial arthritis susceptibility into dichotomous phenotypes.

subject: Jawaheer et al. (2001)
object: Jawaheer et al. (2001) performed a genomewide screen for allele sharing using 379 microsatellite markers in 257 multiplex RA families from the United States, collected by the North American Rheumatoid Arthritis Consortium, that contained 301 affected sib pairs. Nonparametric analysis with SIBPAL confirmed linkage of RA to the HLA locus (P less than 0.00005), with lambda-HLA = 1.79.

subject: Jawaheer et al. (2001)
object: In the same genome screen, Jawaheer et al. (2001) found evidence for linkage at P less than 0.005 to several non-HLA loci, on chromosomes 1 (D1S235), 4 (D4S1647), 12 (D12S373), 16 (D16S403), and 17 (D17S1301). MLOD analysis of X-linked markers with ASPEX also suggested linkage to the telomeric marker DXS6807. Stratifying the families into white or seropositive subgroups revealed some additional markers whose significance improved over the full data set.

subject: Jawaheer et al. (2001)
object: Jawaheer et al. (2001) noted that several regions reaching nominal significance (P less than 0.05) had been implicated earlier in RA (D16S516 and D17S1301) or in other autoimmune diseases. These included systemic lupus erythematosus (D1S235), inflammatory bowel disease (D4S1647, D5S1462, and D16S516), multiple sclerosis (D12S1052), and ankylosing spondylitis (D16S516). The authors concluded that HLA genes play a major role in RA susceptibility but that several other regions also contribute significantly to overall genetic risk, suggesting genetic overlap with other autoimmune diseases.

subject: Yen et al. (2001)
object: Yen et al. (2001) genotyped KIR2DS1 and KIR2DS2 in 76 healthy controls, 70 RA patients without major organ involvement, and 30 RA patients with rheumatoid vasculitis, all Caucasians of Western European descent. KIR2DS2 was present in 83% of patients with rheumatoid vasculitis versus 47% of controls (odds ratio 5.56, P = 0.001) and 39% of patients with uncomplicated RA (odds ratio 7.96, P = 0.001), whereas KIR2DS1 was not associated; the authors concluded that KIR2DS2 did not affect the risk of developing RA but was strongly associated with vascular complications.

subject: Yen et al. (2001)
object: Yen et al. (2001) found that, compared with ethnically matched controls, RA patients had a decreased frequency of HLA-C*04 (OR 0.39) and an increased frequency of HLA-C*05 (OR 2.92). In patients with rheumatoid vasculitis, HLA-C*05 was further increased (OR 5.71, P = 0.001), and HLA-C*03 was enriched exclusively in vasculitis patients (60% positive; OR 3.74, P = 0.003). In logistic regression, HLA-C*03 (OR 8.6) and KIR2DS2 (OR 3.69) each conferred independent risk for vasculitis, with no significant interaction detected.

subject: Yen et al. (2001)
object: Yen et al. (2001) found that CD4+CD28null T-cell clones from 3 patients with rheumatoid vasculitis expressed KIR2DS2 in 58 to 91% of clones, often unopposed by the inhibitory receptors KIR2DL2/KIR2DL3, whereas such clones were rare in healthy controls. Cross-linking of CD158b on KIR2DS2+ clones enhanced IFN-gamma transcription and proliferation in response to suboptimal anti-CD3, and the authors suggested that KIR2DS2 with the appropriate HLA-C ligand may have a role in vascular damage by regulating CD4+CD28null T cells.

subject: Schaller et al. (2001)
object: Schaller et al. (2001) found that 64% of patients with RA, but not controls, had increased concentrations of anti-glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (GPI) IgG in serum and synovial fluid. Concentrations of soluble GPI in the sera and synovial fluids of RA patients were also elevated, which led to immune complex formation.

subject: Schaller et al. (2001)
object: Schaller et al. (2001) cloned, by phage display, a panel of specific high-affinity human monoclonal anti-GPI IgGs from a patient with RA; the antibodies were highly somatically mutated, indicating an affinity-matured, antigen-driven response. Immunohistochemistry of RA synovium showed high concentrations of GPI on the surface of the synovial lining and on the endothelial surface of arterioles, suggesting a mechanism by which anti-GPI antibodies may precipitate joint disease. The authors concluded that the immunologic events leading to arthritis in the K/BxN mouse model may also occur in human RA.

subject: Barton et al. (2001)
object: Barton et al. (2001) studied linkage in rheumatoid arthritis affected sib-pair (ASP) families to 5 human regions homologous to loci found in animal models of inflammatory arthritis. They found linkage to 17q22 in 200 RA ASP families and replicated it in another 100 ASP families. This region is syntenic to a susceptibility locus shared by 2 experimental rat models. Typing additional markers narrowed the linked region to 4 cM.

subject: Barton et al. (2001)
object: Barton et al. (2001) found association between rheumatoid arthritis and marker D17S807 on 17q22 in their ASP cohort, using extensions of the transmission disequilibrium test. In an independent cohort of families with a single RA case, 2 two-marker haplotypes that included D17S807 were associated with RA. This narrowed the region likely to contain the causative mutation to about 1 cM.

subject: Barton et al. (2001)
object: Barton et al. (2001) described rheumatoid arthritis as an oligogenic autoimmune disease. They noted that the only consistent genetic finding had been linkage and association to the MHC, which is estimated to account for only 30 to 40% of the total genetic component of susceptibility.

subject: Leadbetter et al. (2002)
object: Leadbetter et al. (2002) showed that effective activation of B cells expressing rheumatoid factor (RF), an antigen receptor specific for self-IgG, was mediated by IgG2a-chromatin immune complexes and required synergistic engagement of the antigen receptor and a member of the MyD88-dependent Toll-like receptor family; inhibitor studies implicated TLR9. The authors concluded that these data established a critical link between innate and adaptive immunity in the development of systemic autoimmune disease and explained the preponderance of autoantibodies reactive with nucleic acid-protein particles.

subject: Jawaheer et al. (2002)
object: Jawaheer et al. (2002) performed extensive haplotype analysis using 54 markers distributed across the entire HLA complex in 469 multicase families with RA. They found that, in addition to associations with HLA-DRB1 alleles, at least 2 additional genetic effects were present within the MHC. One lay within a 497-kb region in the central portion of the HLA complex, an interval that excludes DRB1, on a segment of the highly conserved ancestral A1-B8-DRB1*03 (8.1) haplotype.

subject: Jawaheer et al. (2002)
object: Jawaheer et al. (2002) suggested that additional risk genes may also be present in the HLA class I region in a subset of DRB1*0404 haplotypes, and concluded that HLA associations with RA are complex and cannot be completely explained by the DRB1 locus.

subject: Okamoto et al. (2003)
object: In Japanese patients with RA and a control group, Okamoto et al. (2003) had earlier reported a second RA susceptibility gene in the telomeric HLA class III region, apart from HLA-DRB1. Using microsatellites, they narrowed the region to 70 kb telomeric of the TNF cluster, which contains 4 expressed genes (IkappaBL, ATP6G, BAT1, and MICB).

subject: Okamoto et al. (2003)
object: Using many SNPs and insertion/deletion polymorphisms, Okamoto et al. (2003) identified the second RA susceptibility locus in the HLA region as the T allele of SNP 96452 (T/A), at position -62 in the promoter of the IkappaBL gene (P = 0.0062), in Japanese patients. The -62T/A SNP disrupts a putative binding motif for the transcriptional repressor deltaEF1, so it may affect IkappaBL transcription. IkappaBL is homologous to IkappaB-alpha, a known inhibitor of NF-kappa-B.

subject: IKAPPABL SNP 96452 (T/A), -62T/A
object: IKAPPABL

subject: Okamoto et al. (2003)
object: Okamoto et al. (2003) suggested that the MHC may contain RA genetic determinants that affect both the innate immune system (through IkappaBL and NF-kappa-B) and the adaptive immune system (through HLA-DRB1).

subject: Nedvetzki et al. (2003)
object: Nedvetzki et al. (2003) found that synovial fluid cells from the joints of patients with rheumatoid arthritis expressed a novel CD44 variant, designated CD44vRA, which carried an extra CAG trinucleotide transcribed from intronic sequences flanking a variant exon. CD44vRA was detected in 23 of 30 RA patients.

subject: CD44 CD44vRA (extra trinucleotide CAG)
object: CD44

subject: Nedvetzki et al. (2003)
object: Nedvetzki et al. (2003) showed that CD44-negative Namalwa cells transfected with CD44vRA or wildtype CD44v3-v10 bound FGF2 equally through heparan sulfate chains, but cells immobilizing FGF2 via CD44vRA bound substantially more soluble FGFR1 and stimulated proliferation of FGFR1-bearing BaF-32 cells more efficiently. Primary RA synovial fluid cells expressing CD44vRA bound more soluble FGFR1 than synovial cells expressing CD44v3-v10 or osteoarthritis synovial cells, and this binding was reduced by antibodies against the CD44 v3 exon product. The authors suggested that this enhanced FGF2–FGFR1 interaction may foster the destructive inflammatory cascade in RA and possibly other autoimmune diseases.

subject: Fisher et al. (2003)
object: Fisher et al. (2003) carried out a genome-search meta-analysis of the published results of 4 genome-wide linkage studies of rheumatoid arthritis. They defined 120 genomic bins of about 30 cM each and ranked them by maximum evidence for linkage. Apart from the HLA locus (P < 0.00002), the strongest evidence for an RA susceptibility locus was on chromosome 16 (P = 0.004). None of the 4 individual genome searches had found this locus to be statistically significant.

subject: Fisher et al. (2003)
object: In the meta-analysis by Fisher et al. (2003), 12 regions reached a significant summed rank (P < 0.05), whereas 6 bins would be expected by chance. Four of these regions, on 6p, 16cen, 6q, and 12p, reached P < 0.01. The authors suggested that a subset of these regions contains RA susceptibility loci.

subject: Suzuki et al. (2003)
object: Suzuki et al. (2003) used a case-control linkage disequilibrium study to show that PADI4, one of 4 PADI genes in a previously linked RA susceptibility region, is a susceptibility locus for rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.000008). They identified a PADI4 haplotype associated with RA susceptibility.

subject: Suzuki et al. (2003)
object: Suzuki et al. (2003) found that the RA-susceptibility PADI4 haplotype affected transcript stability and was associated with levels of antibody to citrullinated peptide in sera from patients with RA. PADI4 was expressed in hematologic tissues and RA synovial tissues. The authors suggested that the susceptibility haplotype increases production of citrullinated peptides that act as autoantigens, heightening risk of disease.

subject: Hill et al. (2003)
object: Hill et al. (2003) noted that rheumatoid arthritis is genetically associated with MHC class II molecules containing the shared epitope, and postulated that these MHC molecules may participate in disease pathogenesis by selectively binding arthritogenic peptides for presentation to autoreactive CD4+ T cells; they noted that posttranslationally modified proteins containing citrulline (deiminated arginine) had recently been identified as specific targets of the IgG antibody response in RA patients.

subject: Hill et al. (2003)
object: To understand how citrulline might evoke an autoimmune reaction, Hill et al. (2003) studied T cell responses to citrulline-containing peptides in HLA-DRB1*0401 transgenic (DR4-IE tg) mice and demonstrated that conversion of arginine to citrulline at the peptide side-chain position interacting with the shared epitope significantly increased peptide-MHC affinity and led to activation of CD4+ T cells in these mice.

subject: Hill et al. (2003)
object: Hill et al. (2003) concluded that their results revealed how DRB1 alleles carrying the shared epitope could initiate an autoimmune response to citrullinated self-antigens in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Lard et al. (2003)
object: Lard et al. (2003) genotyped the -2849 A/G IL10 promoter polymorphism, which is associated with high (AG/GG) and low (AA) IL-10 production, in 283 RA patients, 413 patients with other rheumatic diseases, and 1,220 healthy controls. The IL10 genotype was not associated with the incidence of RA, but was associated with disease progression: patients with the high-IL-10-production genotype had a higher rate of joint destruction and higher baseline autoantibody titers (IgG and IgM rheumatoid factors and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies).

subject: IL10 -2849 A/G
object: IL10

subject: Lard et al. (2003)
object: Lard et al. (2003) found that adenoviral gene transfer of IL10 to fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) inhibited their invasiveness, but FLS invasiveness in vitro did not differ between RA patients who were -2849 G carriers and non-G carriers. They concluded that the -2849 IL10 promoter polymorphism is associated with autoantibody production and subsequent joint damage in RA.

subject: Vandenbroeck et al. (2003)
object: Vandenbroeck et al. (2003) genotyped 4 microsatellite markers in a 118-kb interval containing the IFNG and IL26 genes on chromosome 12q15 in 251 patients with RA and 198 unrelated healthy controls from Northern Ireland. Marker D12S2510, located 3 kb 3-prime of IL26, was significantly associated with RA in women (corrected P = 0.008) but not in men (P = 0.99). A 3-marker haplotype, IFNGCA*13;D12S2510*8;D12S2511*9, was significantly underrepresented in women with RA (odds ratio 0.50; corrected P = 0.03) but not in men. The authors concluded that common polymorphisms in the IFNG/IL26 region may contribute to sex bias in RA susceptibility.

subject: Schönland et al. (2003)
object: Schönland et al. (2003) studied whether HLA-DRB1*04 alleles, the major susceptibility genes for rheumatoid arthritis, confer risk for T-cell senescence. In healthy individuals, HLA-DRB1*04 alleles were associated with excessive loss of telomeres in CD4+ T cells. This accelerated erosion occurred during the first 2 decades of life and was followed by reduced homeostatic T-cell proliferation in adulthood. Telomeric repair mechanisms were intact in HLA-DRB1*04+ donors.

subject: Schönland et al. (2003)
object: Schönland et al. (2003) found that premature telomeric loss also affected granulocytes, which suggested that the hematopoietic stem cell is the primary target. They proposed that HLA-DRB1*04 alleles, or genes in linkage disequilibrium with them, regulate stem cell replication and contribute to the accumulation of senescent and autoreactive T cells in rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Tokuhiro et al. (2003)
object: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) used SNPs in a case-control linkage disequilibrium mapping study of the cytokine gene cluster on chromosome 5q31 in the Japanese population. They found a significant association between rheumatoid arthritis and the organic cation transporter gene SLC22A4 (P = 0.000034).

subject: Tokuhiro et al. (2003)
object: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) found that an intronic SNP in SLC22A4, associated with rheumatoid arthritis, lies in a RUNX1 binding site. In vitro, this SNP affected the transcriptional efficiency of SLC22A4 because the two alleles differed in their affinity for the hematopoietic transcriptional regulator RUNX1.

subject: SLC22A4 intronic SNP in a RUNX1 binding site of SLC22A4
object: SLC22A4

subject: Tokuhiro et al. (2003)
object: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) found that a SNP in RUNX1 was also strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis (P = 0.00035). They concluded that RUNX1 regulation of SLC22A4 expression is associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis and suggested this may be an example of an epistatic effect of two genes on the disorder.

subject: RUNX1 A SNP in RUNX1
object: RUNX1

subject: Tokuhiro et al. (2003)
object: Tokuhiro et al. (2003) showed that SLC22A4 expression is specific to hematological and immunological tissues. SLC22A4 was also highly expressed in the inflamed joints of mice with collagen-induced arthritis.

subject: Sakaguchi et al. (2003)
object: Sakaguchi et al. (2003) found that in mice, a spontaneous point mutation in the gene region encoding an SH2 domain of ZAP-70, a key T-cell signal transduction molecule, caused chronic autoimmune arthritis that resembled human rheumatoid arthritis in many respects.

subject: ZAP70 spontaneous point mutation of the gene encoding an SH2 domain of ZAP-70
object: ZAP70

subject: Sakaguchi et al. (2003)
object: Sakaguchi et al. (2003) reported that altered T-cell receptor signaling through the aberrant ZAP-70 changed the thresholds of T cells to thymic selection. As a result, autoimmune T cells that would otherwise be negatively selected were positively selected. They suggested that thymic production of arthritogenic T cells, caused by a genetically determined shift of the T-cell repertoire toward high self-reactivity, might also be crucial to disease development in a subset of patients with RA.

subject: John et al. (2004)
object: John et al. (2004) carried out a whole-genome linkage screen of 157 families with multiple cases of rheumatoid arthritis using 11,245 genomewide SNPs and compared it with a 10-cM microsatellite scan of the same cohort. The SNP analysis detected the major RA susceptibility locus, HLA-DRB1 (P = 0.00004), with a linkage interval of 31 cM, compared with 50 cM in the microsatellite scan. Four more loci reached nominal significance (P less than 0.05) in the SNP analysis but were not seen in the microsatellite scan.

subject: John et al. (2004)
object: John et al. (2004) found that differences between the SNP and microsatellite scans were mainly due to information content, which was significantly higher for the SNPs. When the SNP set was reduced to 3,300 markers (1-cM spacing), several loci fell below nominal significance. Map differences, genotyping error and moderate linkage disequilibrium between markers did not significantly affect the results.

subject: Begovich et al. (2004)
object: Begovich et al. (2004) tested putative functional SNPs for association with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in white individuals using a case-control design, then tested a second sample for replication. They found that the minor allele of a missense SNP in PTPN22, which encodes the hematopoietic-specific protein tyrosine phosphatase Lyp, was associated with RA susceptibility (discovery-study allelic P = 6.6 x 10(-4); replication-study allelic P = 5.6 x 10(-8)). The risk allele was present in about 28% of white individuals with RA and about 17% of white individuals from the general population.

subject: PTPN22 minor allele of a missense SNP in PTPN22
object: PTPN22

subject: Begovich et al. (2004)
object: Begovich et al. (2004) showed that the PTPN22 risk allele disrupts the P1 proline-rich motif, which is important for interaction with Csk. They noted this could alter the normal function of these proteins as negative regulators of T-cell activation. Because the same allele had recently been implicated in type 1 diabetes, the authors suggested that the variant phosphatase may increase overall immune reactivity and raise a carrier's risk of autoimmune disease.

subject: Begovich et al. (2004)
object: Begovich et al. (2004) described rheumatoid arthritis as the most common systemic autoimmune disease, affecting about 1% of adults worldwide, with an estimated heritability of 60%.

subject: Seo et al. (2004)
object: Seo et al. (2004) noted that collagen type II-induced arthritis, a CD4+ T-cell-dependent chronic inflammation of susceptible DBA/1 mice, represents an animal model of human rheumatoid arthritis, and found that both the development of this condition and even established disease were inhibited by an agonistic anti-4-1BB monoclonal antibody.

subject: Seo et al. (2004)
object: Seo et al. (2004) reported that anti-4-1BB antibody suppressed serum antibodies to collagen type II and CD4+ T-cell recall responses to collagen type II, and that crosslinking of 4-1BB evoked an antigen-specific, active suppression mechanism that differed from the results of blocking the interaction between 4-1BB and its ligand, 4-1BBL.

subject: Seo et al. (2004)
object: Seo et al. (2004) found that anti-4-1BB monoclonal antibodies induced massive, antigen-dependent clonal expansion of CD11c+CD8+ T cells and accumulation of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase in CD11b+ monocytes and CD11c+ dendritic cells, and that both anti-interferon-gamma and 1-methyltryptophan, a pharmacological inhibitor of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, reversed the anti-4-1BB effect. The authors concluded that suppression of collagen-induced arthritis was caused by expansion of new CD11c+CD8+ T cells and that interferon-gamma produced by these cells suppresses antigen-specific CD4+ T cells through an indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase-dependent mechanism.

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: Lundberg et al. (2005) showed in female Lew.1AV1 rats that immunisation with citrullinated rat serum albumin (Cit-RSA), but not with unmodified rat serum albumin (RSA), induced an IgG antibody response against the citrullinated protein that cross-reacted with the native protein at all time points examined (12, 24, 35 and 61 days after immunisation; n = 7 per group), indicating that citrullination of a non-immunogenic self antigen broke B cell tolerance.

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: Lundberg et al. (2005) found that lymph node cells taken 10 days after immunisation from Lew.1AV1 rats immunised with Cit-RSA proliferated significantly more strongly in response to Cit-RSA than did cells from RSA-immunised rats (P < 0.05), with a similar but non-significant trend on stimulation with unmodified RSA; the authors concluded that RSA with strong adjuvant can induce an autoreactive T cell response insufficient for B cell help, whereas Cit-RSA induced a stronger T cell response capable of conferring B cell help.

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: In the rat collagen-induced arthritis model, Lundberg et al. (2005) reported that immunisation of Lew.1AV1 rats with citrullinated rat collagen type II (Cit-CII) induced arthritis with significantly higher incidence (35% higher in the early phase, 15% higher at end stage) and earlier onset (day 13 versus day 16 after immunisation) than the same amount of unmodified CII (20 animals per group), with a non-significant trend toward higher mean arthritis score; given the low arginine content of CII the authors concluded that conversion of arginine to citrulline is a highly potent mechanism for increased autoreactivity.

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: Using immunohistochemistry on ankle joint synovial tissue of male Dark Agouti rats with collagen-induced arthritis, Lundberg et al. (2005) demonstrated for the first time the kinetics of citrullinated proteins in arthritic joints: citrulline staining (with the RA-patient-derived recombinant antibody RA3, confirmed with anti-modified-citrulline antibodies) first appeared after disease onset at day 21 after immunisation and increased as disease became more severe and chronic (days 28 and 38), while unimmunised animals and all earlier time points including the day of onset (day 15) were negative; staining was mainly in extracellular deposits, presumably fibrin, but also in infiltrating cells and on the cartilage surface, and was joint-specific (lung, ear, spinal cord, spleen, lymph nodes and salivary glands were negative).

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: Lundberg et al. (2005) detected the citrullinating enzyme PAD4 in synovial tissue of rats with collagen-induced arthritis from 21 days after immunisation, localised to the cytoplasm of infiltrating mononuclear cells, with increasing numbers of positive cells by days 28 and 38; PAD4 was not detectable in healthy synovium or at days 3, 6, 10 or 15 after immunisation despite apparent inflammation at day 15, and its amount correlated with severity of inflammation.

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: From these findings Lundberg et al. (2005) concluded that citrullination can break tolerance against the ubiquitous self antigen rat serum albumin and increase the arthritogenicity of the tissue-specific protein collagen type II, and because citrullinated proteins and PAD4 were not detectable in joints before clinical arthritis they postulated that in this model citrullination is a result rather than an initiator of inflammation; they hypothesised that in individuals with the appropriate genetic background a subclinical inflammation, possibly occurring outside the joints (for example smoking-induced lung inflammation in carriers of the MHC shared epitope), induces citrullination of endogenous proteins and generation of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies that potentiate an inflammatory trigger in joints and thereby initiate RA.

subject: Lundberg et al. (2005)
object: Lundberg et al. (2005) noted that an immune response towards any citrullinated protein is clearly not sufficient to induce clinical arthritis, since Cit-RSA-immunised rats, despite developing anti-citrullinated protein antibodies, showed no signs of disease, and that both genetic and environmental factors most probably contribute to arthritis development.

subject: Tamiya et al. (2005)
object: Tamiya et al. (2005) carried out a whole-genome association study of rheumatoid arthritis. They used 27,039 microsatellites spaced at about 100-kb intervals and DNA pooling across three successive genomic screens of independent case-control populations, then fine-mapped candidate regions by SNP analysis. They identified 47 candidate regions. The top 7 loci withstood the most stringent statistical tests and were narrowed down to individual genes and/or SNPs on 4 chromosomes, including the previously known HLA-DRB1 gene on 6p21.3.

subject: Tamiya et al. (2005)
object: Tamiya et al. (2005) noted that rheumatoid arthritis is a destructive joint disease that affects up to 1% of the population.

subject: Camps et al. (2005)
object: Camps et al. (2005) found that Pik3cg-null mice, which lack PI3Kgamma, were largely protected in mouse models of rheumatoid arthritis, and that this protection correlated with defective neutrophil migration.

subject: Camps et al. (2005)
object: Camps et al. (2005) developed specific, selective, orally active small-molecule inhibitors of PI3Kgamma. Oral treatment with a PI3Kgamma inhibitor slowed the progression of joint inflammation and damage in 2 different mouse models of rheumatoid arthritis, matching the protection seen in Pik3cg-null mice. The authors proposed selective PI3Kgamma inhibitors as possible treatments for chronic inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Carlton et al. (2005)
object: Carlton et al. (2005) sequenced the coding regions of PTPN22 in 48 white North American patients with RA and identified 15 previously unreported SNPs, including 2 coding SNPs in the catalytic domain. They then genotyped 37 SNPs in or near PTPN22 in 475 RA patients and 475 individually matched controls, and replicated a subset in 661 patients and 1,322 matched controls; the sole haplotype carrying the W620 risk allele (R620W, rs2476601) was strongly associated with disease in both sample sets, whereas a haplotype identical at all other SNPs but carrying R620 showed no association.

subject: PTPN22 p.R620W
object: PTPN22

subject: Carlton et al. (2005)
object: Carlton et al. (2005) found that R620W does not fully explain the association between PTPN22 and RA, since significant case-control differences persisted in both sample sets after stratification by R620W; two SNPs on a single common haplotype were associated with RA independent of R620W, suggesting that R620W and at least one additional variant in the PTPN22 gene region influence RA susceptibility.

subject: Carlton et al. (2005)
object: Carlton et al. (2005) predicted 10 common (frequency greater than 1%) PTPN22 haplotypes in white North Americans.

subject: Seyler et al. (2005)
object: Seyler et al. (2005) examined 72 rheumatoid synovial tissues representing 3 types of synovitis (ectopic germinal center (GC)-containing, T cell-B cell aggregates without GC reactions, and diffuse infiltrates). GC+ synovitis had the highest levels of APRIL, produced exclusively by CD83+ dendritic cells, whereas BLyS was present at similar levels in all tissue types and derived exclusively from CD68+ macrophages.

subject: Seyler et al. (2005)
object: Seyler et al. (2005) treated human synovium-SCID mouse chimeras with the APRIL/BLyS decoy receptor TACI:Fc. In GC+ synovitis, treatment caused GC destruction and marked inhibition of IFN-gamma and Ig transcription, whereas in aggregate and diffuse synovitis Ig levels were unaffected and IFN-gamma production was enhanced; these differential effects correlated with the presence of TACI+ T cells in aggregate and diffuse synovitis and their absence in GC+ synovitis. The authors proposed that BLyS and APRIL regulate B cell as well as T cell function and have pro- and antiinflammatory activities in RA.

subject: Amos et al. (2006)
object: Amos et al. (2006) did a genome-wide linkage scan with more than 5,700 informative SNP markers (Illumina IV SNP linkage panel) in 642 Caucasian families with affected sib pairs with rheumatoid arthritis, ascertained by the North American Rheumatoid Arthritis Consortium. They found new evidence of linkage at chromosomes 2q33 (lod score of 3.52) and 11p12 (lod score of 3.09).

subject: Amos et al. (2006)
object: Amos et al. (2006) also found a strong, broad linkage interval around the major histocompatibility complex (lod score greater than 16), regions on chromosomes 5 and 10 with lod scores above 2.5, and further evidence of linkage (lod scores 1.46 to 2.35) on chromosomes 4, 7, 12, 16, and 18. They attributed the new evidence partly to the higher information content of the SNP panel (75.6%) compared with a microsatellite panel used previously (mean 52.6%).

subject: Amos et al. (2006)
object: Amos et al. (2006) stratified sib pairs by whether or not they had elevated anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) titers. They found that the evidence for linkage on chromosomes 4, 5, 6, and 7 varied significantly between strata.

subject: Rizzo et al. (2006)
object: Rizzo et al. (2006) found that the HLA-G 14-bp deletion/insertion polymorphism was associated with methotrexate (MTX) response in RA: the -14/-14 bp genotype was increased among MTX responders compared with nonresponders (chi-square = 6.12, P = 0.02; odds ratio = 2.46, 95% CI 1.26-4.84, P = 0.009 by logistic regression). The authors proposed this polymorphism as a therapy marker in the early phases of the disease.

subject: HLA-G 14-bp deletion/insertion polymorphism, -14/-14 bp genotype
object: HLA-G

subject: Rizzo et al. (2006)
object: Rizzo et al. (2006) showed that activation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from healthy individuals and non-MTX-treated RA patients with methotrexate induced production of soluble HLA-G, with the highest sHLA-G1 concentrations significantly associated with the HLA-G -14/-14 bp genotype. They proposed that MTX induces anti-inflammatory sHLA-G molecules that contribute to the therapeutic response.

subject: HLA-G -14/-14 bp genotype
object: HLA-G

subject: Kawane et al. (2006)
object: Kawane et al. (2006) found that Dnase2/Ifnar1 double-knockout mice (DNase II-/- IFN-IR-/-) and mice with an induced deletion of the DNase II gene developed a chronic polyarthritis resembling human rheumatoid arthritis. A set of cytokine genes was strongly activated in the affected joints. The mice's serum contained high levels of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, rheumatoid factor, and matrix metalloproteinase-3.

subject: Kawane et al. (2006)
object: Kawane et al. (2006) found that early in disease, expression of the gene encoding TNF-alpha was upregulated in the bone marrow of DNase II-deficient mice. Giving the mice anti-TNF-alpha antibody prevented arthritis. The authors concluded that when macrophages cannot degrade mammalian DNA from erythroid precursors and apoptotic cells, they produce TNF-alpha. They proposed that TNF-alpha activates synovial cells to produce various cytokines, leading to chronic polyarthritis.

subject: Kallberg et al. (2007)
object: Kallberg et al. (2007) studied interaction between HLA-DRB1 shared epitope (SE) alleles and the PTPN22 R620W allele in 3 case-control studies: the Swedish EIRA, the North American NARAC, and the Dutch Leiden Early Arthritis Clinic study, totaling 1,977 cases and 2,405 controls. When interaction was defined as departure from additivity, all 3 studies showed consistent interaction between HLA-DRB1 SE alleles and the A allele of PTPN22 R620W for anti-CCP-positive RA. A multiplicative interaction was seen only when the 3 studies were pooled. The linkage disequilibrium approach indicated gene-gene interaction in EIRA and NARAC and in the pooled analysis.

subject: Kallberg et al. (2007)
object: In the Swedish EIRA study, Kallberg et al. (2007) found no interaction between smoking and PTPN22 R620W. The authors described a new pattern of interactions between the 2 major known genetic risk factors (HLA-DRB1 SE and PTPN22) and the major environmental risk factor (smoking) for the risk of anti-CCP-positive RA, which extended the basis for a pathogenetic hypothesis involving genetic and environmental factors.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007)
object: In a genome-wide association study of about 2,000 British Caucasian patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 3,000 shared controls typed with the Affymetrix 500K chip, Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) confirmed strong association with the MHC/HLA-DRB1 region on chromosome 6p21. The strongest MHC SNP was rs6457617 (trend P = 3.44 x 10(-76)). The cases met the 1987 American College of Rheumatology criteria.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) found strong association between rheumatoid arthritis and the PTPN22 SNP rs6679677 on chromosome 1p13 (trend P = 4.9 x 10(-26); heterozygote OR 1.98, homozygote OR 3.32). This SNP is perfectly correlated (HapMap CEU r2 = 1) with the functional SNP rs2476601, and the effect size agreed with previous estimates. The authors noted that the HLA-DRB1 and PTPN22 associations together explain about 50% of the familial aggregation of RA.

subject: PTPN22 rs6679677
object: PTPN22

subject: PTPN22 rs2476601
object: PTPN22

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007)
object: Among the seven diseases studied, rheumatoid arthritis was the only one for which a sex-differentiated analysis produced a strong signal. Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) found that SNP rs11761231 on chromosome 7q32 gave P = 3.9 x 10(-7) on the 2-df sex-differentiated test. The SNP had no effect in males (P = 0.68) but an additive effect in females (P = 6.8 x 10(-8); OR 1.32). The authors advised caution because the SNP is surrounded by recombination hotspots and has no correlated SNPs on the chip, and they suggested it may represent one of the first sex-differentiated effects in human disease.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) found moderate evidence (P between 10(-5) and 5 x 10(-7)) of rheumatoid arthritis association at 9 SNPs, none of which lay at previously reported RA loci. These included SNPs near IL2RA (rs2104286) and IL2RB (rs743777). When RA and type 1 diabetes cases were combined, the IL2RA/CD25 region on 10p15 reached P = 5 x 10(-8).

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) reported data that add variants around IL2RA (10p15), PTPN2 (18p11) and the 12q24 region to the loci shared by rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes. All three appeared to be new for RA. At PTPN2 the RA association was weak (P = 1.9 x 10(-2)), but the combined P value for Crohn disease, RA and type 1 diabetes was 9 x 10(-8). The 12q24 variant gave a combined P value of 9.3 x 10(-10) across all autoimmune cases.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) found moderate evidence of rheumatoid arthritis association at SNP rs6920220 on 6q23 (trend P = 4.99 x 10(-6)). Weaker signals (P between 10(-4) and 10(-5)) were seen in TNFAIP2 (rs2771369), GZMB (rs854350), PRKCQ (rs4750316) and KAZALD1 (rs10786617); the authors suggested that KAZALD1 might be relevant to bone erosions in RA. Two CTLA4 SNPs were only nominally significant (P = 0.085 and 0.034).

subject: Sigurdsson et al. (2007)
object: Sigurdsson et al. (2007) analyzed 5 SNPs in IRF5 and 3 SNPs in TYK2 in a Swedish cohort of 1,530 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 881 controls. Four of the 5 SNPs in the 5-prime region of IRF5 were associated with RA, whereas no association was observed with the TYK2 SNPs. The minor alleles of 3 IRF5 SNPs, which were in linkage disequilibrium and formed a relatively common haplotype (frequency approximately 0.33), appeared to confer protection against RA.

subject: Sigurdsson et al. (2007)
object: Sigurdsson et al. (2007) found that the IRF5 associations with RA were seen in the entire patient group but were mainly found in patients negative for anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies; a suggestive association of IRF5 SNPs with anti-CCP-negative RA was also observed in a Dutch replication cohort of 387 patients and 181 controls. The authors concluded that IRF5 variants contribute to a unique disease etiology and pathogenesis in anti-CCP-negative RA.

subject: Plenge et al. (2007)
object: Plenge et al. (2007) performed a genomewide association study of 317,503 SNPs in 1,522 anti-CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis cases and 1,850 matched controls. Samples came from the North American Rheumatoid Arthritis Consortium (NARAC) and the Swedish EIRA study. SNPs with P<1x10(-8) were then genotyped in an independent replication set of 997 cases and 1,777 controls. In all samples tested, they observed association with the MHC locus, with PTPN22, and with SNP rs3761847 on chromosome 9 (odds ratio 1.32; 95% CI 1.23-1.42; P = 4 x 10(-14)).

subject: TRAF1 rs3761847
object: TRAF1

subject: Plenge et al. (2007)
object: Plenge et al. (2007) found that the associated SNP rs3761847 is in linkage disequilibrium with 2 genes relevant to chronic inflammation: TRAF1 (tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 1) and C5 (complement component 5). They concluded that a common genetic variant at the TRAF1-C5 locus on chromosome 9 is associated with an increased risk of anti-CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Remmers et al. (2007)
object: Remmers et al. (2007) tested SNPs in and around 13 candidate genes within the previously linked chromosome 2q region for association with rheumatoid arthritis, then performed fine mapping of the STAT1-STAT4 region in 1,620 North American patients with established rheumatoid arthritis and 2,635 controls.

subject: Remmers et al. (2007)
object: Remmers et al. (2007) found that a SNP haplotype in the third intron of STAT4, marked by rs7574865, was associated with susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis: the minor alleles were present on 27% of chromosomes of North American patients with established RA vs 22% of controls (P = 2.81 x 10(-7); odds ratio 1.32). The association was replicated in an independent Swedish series of 1,529 patients with early (recent-onset) RA and 881 matched controls (P = 0.02).

subject: STAT4 rs7574865
object: STAT4

subject: Remmers et al. (2007)
object: Remmers et al. (2007) reported that homozygosity for the STAT4 risk allele, compared with absence of the allele, was associated with a 60% increased risk for rheumatoid arthritis and a more than doubled risk for systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Remmers et al. (2007)
object: Remmers et al. (2007) found that the STAT4 haplotype marked by rs7574865 was also strongly associated with systemic lupus erythematosus in 1,039 patients and 1,248 controls from 3 series (31% vs 22% of chromosomes; P = 1.87 x 10(-9); odds ratio 1.55), suggesting a shared pathway for rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.

subject: Thomson et al. (2007)
object: Thomson et al. (2007) genotyped 9 SNPs that the WTCCC genome-wide association screen had putatively associated with rheumatoid arthritis (P = 1 x 10(-5) to 5 x 10(-7)) in an independent UK cohort of 5,063 RA cases and 3,849 healthy controls. One SNP, rs6920220 (G>A), was replicated (OR for the minor allele = 1.23; 95% CI 1.15-1.33; trend P = 1.1 x 10(-8)). In a combined analysis with the WTCCC data, the trend P value was 3.6 x 10(-12) (OR = 1.22). The SNP maps to an intergenic region of 6q23, between the OLIG3 and TNFAIP3 genes.

subject: Thomson et al. (2007)
object: Thomson et al. (2007) found that rs6920220 lies in a 60-kb linkage disequilibrium block that contains no known genes but includes part of a PTPN11 pseudogene. The block lies between OLIG3 and TNFAIP3 (A20). The authors noted that TNFAIP3 negatively regulates NF-kappa-B and that TNFAIP3-deficient mice develop multiorgan inflammation, including inflammation of the joints.

subject: Thomson et al. (2007)
object: Thomson et al. (2007) found that the rs6920220 association was stronger in RA patients with antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) and in rheumatoid factor-positive patients. In the WTCCC data, the OR was 1.38 in anti-CCP-positive patients and 1.03 in anti-CCP-negative patients. In the combined cohorts, the difference between the anti-CCP-positive and -negative subgroups was significant (trend P = 0.003). The authors suggested that RA may comprise at least 2 genetically distinct subsets.

subject: Thomson et al. (2007)
object: Thomson et al. (2007) found no interaction between rs6920220 and the HLA-DRB1 or PTPN22 susceptibility markers, suggesting that this variant has an independent effect. Together, the HLA-DRB1 shared epitope, PTPN22 rs2476601, and rs6920220 accounted for 8.5% of the total variance in RA susceptibility. The PTPN22 rs2476601 association was also confirmed in this cohort (OR = 1.53; trend P = 2.0 x 10(-18)).

subject: Thomson et al. (2007)
object: Thomson et al. (2007) found modest evidence of association with RA for rs743777 in IL2RB (combined trend P = 5.3 x 10(-6); OR = 1.13). Evidence for the reported sex-differentiated effect of rs11761231 near PODXL was only borderline (trend P = 0.042). The IL2RA SNP rs2104286 was not associated with RA in this dataset.

subject: IL2RB rs743777
object: IL2RB

subject: PODXL rs11761231
object: PODXL

subject: IL2RA rs2104286
object: IL2RA

subject: Plenge et al. (2007)
object: Plenge et al. (2007) genotyped 397 individuals with rheumatoid arthritis for 116,204 SNPs. They compared these data with publicly available genotype data for 1,211 related individuals from the Framingham Heart Study. After adjusting for technical and population biases, they found a SNP at 6q23 (rs10499194), about 150 kb from TNFAIP3 and OLIG3, that was reproducibly associated with rheumatoid arthritis. The association was seen in the GWA scan (P = 10(-3)) and in 5,541 additional case-control samples (P < 10(-6)), giving a combined P of 10(-9).

subject: Plenge et al. (2007)
object: Plenge et al. (2007) noted that the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (WTCCC) had reported an association between rheumatoid arthritis and a different SNP, rs6920220, located 3.8 kb from rs10499194. Plenge et al. (2007) showed that the two SNP associations were statistically independent and were each reproducible when their data were compared with the WTCCC data. Together, the two SNPs defined risk and protective haplotypes for rheumatoid arthritis at 6q23.

subject: Martínez et al. (2008)
object: Martínez et al. (2008) genotyped the STAT4 tagging polymorphism rs7574865 by TaqMan assay in 575 Spanish patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 723 ethnically matched healthy controls. They confirmed the association with RA (T vs G allele, P = 1.2 x 10(-6); odds ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.31-1.92).

subject: Martínez et al. (2008)
object: In the same Spanish cohort, Martínez et al. (2008) also found an association of STAT4 rs7574865 with inflammatory bowel disease, covering both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (T vs G, P = 0.006; OR 1.29). They also found an association with type 1 diabetes (P = 0.008; OR 1.36). They found no association with multiple sclerosis (P = 0.83). The authors concluded that STAT4 is emerging as a common risk factor for diverse complex diseases.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) carried out a meta-analysis of two published genome-wide association studies of rheumatoid arthritis (3,393 cases and 12,462 controls of European ancestry, from the WTCCC, EIRA and NARAC collections). They then genotyped 31 top-ranked SNPs not previously associated with rheumatoid arthritis in an independent replication set of 3,929 autoantibody-positive cases and 5,807 matched controls from 8 collections. Six of the 31 SNPs reached P of 0.01 or less in replication, which was significantly more than expected by chance.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) identified an association between rheumatoid arthritis and SNP rs4810485 at chromosome 20q13, located in the second intron of the CD40 gene (overall P = 8.2 x 10(-9); replication P = 0.0032; odds ratio 0.87 for the minor T allele). rs4810485 is in near-perfect linkage disequilibrium (r2 = 0.95) with rs1883832, a variant that has been associated with autoimmune thyroid disease and has been shown to affect the efficiency of CD40 protein translation by disrupting a Kozak sequence. The same allele contributes to risk in both diseases.

subject: CD40 rs4810485
object: CD40

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) identified an association between rheumatoid arthritis and SNP rs2812378 at chromosome 9p13, located about 0.1 kb from the 5-prime untranslated region of CCL21 (replication P = 0.00097; overall P = 2.8 x 10(-7); joint odds ratio 1.12). The SNP lies in a linkage disequilibrium block that includes the whole CCL21 coding sequence but not the nearby genes. CCL21 is a chemokine involved in homing lymphocytes to secondary lymphoid organs.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008)
object: In their genome-wide association meta-analysis, Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) observed association at the previously confirmed rheumatoid arthritis risk loci PTPN22, 6q23 (TNFAIP3), STAT4 and TRAF1-C5. They also observed association at 4q27 (IL2/IL21), which they described as an independent replication, and at CTLA4, but not at PADI4.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) concluded that the association at CD40, together with the associations near TRAF1 and TNFAIP3, gave strong evidence for a central role of the CD40 signaling pathway in autoantibody-positive rheumatoid arthritis. They suggested that this pathway may act through NF-kappa-B activation, and noted that CD40 stimulation drives B-cell proliferation by regulating CDK6 expression.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) estimated that the newly identified variants together explained only 0.6% of the variance in rheumatoid arthritis risk, and that all known non-MHC common variants explained 3.6%. Given that about 60% of rheumatoid arthritis risk is thought to be genetic, with one-third of that from the MHC, they concluded that less than half of the genetic variation is explained by known risk alleles. They suggested that further common alleles of modest effect remain to be found.

subject: Suzuki et al. (2008)
object: Suzuki et al. (2008) identified a linkage disequilibrium block associated with rheumatoid arthritis in the chromosome 1q region containing multiple SLAM family genes. Within this block, the association peaked at two functional SNPs in CD244, rs3766379 and rs6682654, in two independent rheumatoid arthritis cohorts from Japan (P = 3.23 x 10(-8) and P = 7.45 x 10(-8)).

subject: Suzuki et al. (2008)
object: Suzuki et al. (2008) demonstrated that the rheumatoid arthritis-susceptible alleles of the CD244 SNPs rs3766379 and rs6682654, and their haplotype, increased expression in luciferase and allele-specific transcript quantification assays. The authors concluded that CD244 is a genetic risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis.

subject: Suzuki et al. (2008)
object: Suzuki et al. (2008) found that a Japanese cohort with systemic lupus erythematosus had a CD244 genotype distribution similar to that of the rheumatoid arthritis cohorts. They suggested that CD244 may have a role in the autoimmune process shared by rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

subject: Barton et al. (2009)
object: Barton et al. (2009) genotyped 18 SNPs at 14 loci previously suggested to be type 1 diabetes susceptibility loci in 3,962 UK RA cases and 3,531 unrelated UK controls. They identified an association between RA and SNP rs10865035 at the AFF3 locus on chromosome 2. Combined with WTCCC data (proxy SNP rs9653442) and an inception cohort, the analysis included 6,819 RA cases and 12,650 controls and gave OR 1.12 (95% CI 1.07-1.17), P = 2.8 x 10(-7). The associated variants map to the 5-prime and promoter region of AFF3, which is preferentially expressed in lymphoid cells.

subject: Orozco et al. (2009)
object: Orozco et al. (2009) fine-mapped the 6q23 RA susceptibility locus by genotyping 70 SNPs in 3,962 UK RA patients of Northern European descent and 3,531 healthy controls, and found 18 SNPs associated with RA. The strongest association was with rs6920220 (P = 2.61 x 10(-7), OR 1.22), located in an intergenic region between OLIG3 and TNFAIP3, and haplotype 1, tagged by rs6920220, conferred risk for RA.

subject: Orozco et al. (2009)
object: Orozco et al. (2009) found that the next most strongly associated SNP at 6q23 was rs13207033 (P = 0.0001, OR 0.86), which was perfectly correlated with rs10499194; the minor allele was protective. The authors stated that this was the first independent replication of the association of rs10499194 with RA susceptibility.

subject: Orozco et al. (2009)
object: Orozco et al. (2009) identified a new potential RA marker, rs5029937, in intron 2 of TNFAIP3. Conditional logistic regression showed that only rs6920220, rs13207033, and rs5029937 stayed significant, which suggests 3 independent effects. In pooled data with the WTCCC GWAS, rs5029937 remained highly significant after conditioning on both other SNPs (P = 7.59 x 10(-6)). The authors said replication in an independent cohort was needed.

subject: Orozco et al. (2009)
object: Orozco et al. (2009) found that carrying the risk alleles of both rs6920220 and rs5029937, together with absence of the protective allele of rs13207033, was strongly associated with RA compared with carrying none of them (OR 1.86). This equated to an effect size of 1.50 compared with controls, higher than for any single SNP. The high-risk combination was carried by 4.4% of patients and 2.3% of controls.

subject: Orozco et al. (2009)
object: Orozco et al. (2009) found that rs6920220 and rs5029937 appeared to be associated with autoantibody-positive RA, with strong association in both RF-positive and anti-CCP-positive cases. In contrast, rs13207033 was associated with both RF-positive and RF-negative cases but only with anti-CCP-negative cases. All 3 SNPs were associated in both male and female patients.

subject: Orozco et al. (2009)
object: Orozco et al. (2009) found that the functional exon 3 TNFAIP3 polymorphism rs2230926, which had been associated with SLE, was not independently associated with RA in their study.

subject: Gregersen et al. (2009)
object: Gregersen et al. (2009) carried out a genome-wide association study of rheumatoid arthritis in 2,418 cases and 4,504 controls of European origin from North America; about 95% of the cases were positive for anti-CCP antibodies. They found an association at the REL locus on chromosome 2p13 for rs13031237 (P = 6.01 x 10(-10)) and rs13017599 (P = 9.05 x 10(-9)). After PTPN22, this was the second most significant non-MHC signal. In replication sets of 2,604 cases and 2,882 controls from the US and Canada, the association was confirmed. In the combined data, the allelic OR was 1.25 for rs13031237 (P = 3.08 x 10(-14)) and 1.21 for rs13017599 (P = 2.60 x 10(-11)).

Testing all pairwise interactions between SNPs in CTLA4, REL and BLK identified no significant gene-gene interaction after correction for multiple testing.

subject: Gregersen et al. (2009)
object: Gregersen et al. (2009) suggested that the associations at CD40, REL, TRAF1 and TNFAIP3 point to an important role for CD40 signaling pathways in rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis. They noted that c-Rel regulates T-cell genes including CD40 and TNFAIP3 and, like PRKCQ, is involved in the survival of activated CD8 cells.

subject: Gregersen et al. (2009)
object: Gregersen et al. (2009) noted that 50 to 80% of patients meeting standard criteria for rheumatoid arthritis have anti-CCP antibodies. The classical HLA-DRB1 associations, and many other reported genetic associations, are restricted to this subgroup. They also noted evidence for genetic heterogeneity in rheumatoid arthritis risk among racial groups.

subject: Mahdi et al. (2009)
object: In 1,497 individuals from 3 RA cohorts, Mahdi et al. (2009) found antibodies to the immunodominant citrullinated alpha-enolase CEP-1 epitope in 43 to 63% of anti-CCP-positive individuals. This subset was preferentially linked to HLA-DRB1*04.

subject: Mahdi et al. (2009)
object: In a case-control analysis of 1,000 RA patients and 872 controls, Mahdi et al. (2009) found that the combined effect of HLA-DRB1 shared epitope alleles, PTPN22 and smoking was most strongly associated with the anti-CEP-1-positive subset of RA (odds ratio 37). The corresponding anti-CEP-1-negative, anti-CCP-positive subset had an odds ratio of 2. The authors concluded that citrullinated alpha-enolase is a specific citrullinated autoantigen that links smoking to genetic risk factors in the development of RA.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009) took 370 SNPs from 179 independent loci with P < 0.001 in a published RA GWAS meta-analysis of 3,393 cases and 12,462 controls. They used GRAIL, a text-mining method, to score these loci for functional relationships to genes in 16 established RA loci, and 22 loci scored as significantly connected. They genotyped 22 representative SNPs in an independent set of 7,957 autoantibody-positive cases and 11,958 matched controls of European ancestry. Seven SNPs replicated at a Bonferroni-corrected threshold (P < 0.0023).

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009) confirmed an association of RA with rs11586238 on 1p13.1, near the CD2 and CD58 genes (replication P = 1.4 x 10(-6); overall P = 1.0 x 10(-9); OR 1.13 for the minor G allele). The SNP lies 50 kb upstream of the CD2 start site and is also near CD58 and IGSF2.

There was minimal linkage disequilibrium with the known CTLA4-region RA risk SNP rs3087243, and conditional analysis showed that the two SNPs confer RA risk independently.

object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009) found that the 7 replicated SNPs had consistent effects across all 14 collections, with no evidence of heterogeneity. They also found no significant epistatic interactions among the replicated SNPs and the known RA risk alleles.

subject: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009)
object: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009) noted that several of the new RA loci lie in regions already associated with other autoimmune diseases. These were FCGR2A (systemic lupus erythematosus), TAGAP (celiac disease and type 1 diabetes), PTPRC (multiple sclerosis), PRDM1 (Crohn disease) and CD58 (multiple sclerosis). The authors suggested that the loci point to T-cell activation, NF-kappa-B signaling, and B-cell activation and differentiation in RA pathogenesis.

subject: Boilard et al. (2010)
object: Boilard et al. (2010) used flow cytometry to find platelet microparticles (CD41-positive, submicrometer vesicles) in synovial fluid from all 20 patients with rheumatoid arthritis tested, averaging just under 2 x 10(5) per microliter. These microparticles were undetectable in 19 of 20 osteoarthritis synovial fluid samples. Platelet microparticles were also present in synovial fluid from patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and gout. Microparticles from neutrophils, T cells, and macrophages were present in much smaller amounts.

subject: Boilard et al. (2010)
object: Boilard et al. (2010) found that platelet microparticles stimulated synovial fibroblasts to produce IL-6 and IL-8. This applied both to microparticles produced by collagen stimulation of platelets and to microparticles isolated from rheumatoid arthritis synovial fluid. The effect depended on IL-1: microparticles from mice lacking Il1a and Il1b, and fibroblasts lacking the IL-1 receptor, failed to produce the response. Blocking both IL-1-alpha and IL-1-beta was needed to fully neutralize the effect, and IL-1-alpha predominated in the microparticles. The authors suggested that this may help explain the limited effect of IL-1 blockade in RA.

subject: Boilard et al. (2010)
object: In the K/BxN serum-transfer mouse model of inflammatory arthritis, Boilard et al. (2010) found that depleting platelets markedly reduced arthritis, as measured by both clinical scores and histology. Arthritis was not affected by loss or blockade of thromboxane synthase, the thromboxane receptor, or GPIb.

subject: Boilard et al. (2010)
object: Boilard et al. (2010) showed that the collagen receptor glycoprotein VI (GPVI) and the Fc receptor gamma chain were the main mediators of platelet microparticle release when platelets were co-cultured with fibroblast-like synoviocytes. After K/BxN serum transfer, arthritis was significantly reduced in Gp6-null mice. The authors noted that antagonizing GPVI could be a new therapeutic approach.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010)
object: In a genome-wide association study of 3,432 polymorphic CNVs in about 2,000 UK cases each of 8 common diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, and about 3,000 shared controls, Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010) found a CNV in the HLA region associated with rheumatoid arthritis (CNVR2845.14; p = 1.4 x 10(-39); OR = 1.77). They had no evidence that the HLA CNVs associated with autoimmune diseases were signals independent of the known associated HLA haplotypes.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010) found a CNV (CNVR1065.1) that is annotated as mapping uniquely to chromosome 2 and showed a strong association with rheumatoid arthritis (p = 6.8 x 10(-49); OR = 1.85) and type 1 diabetes. They showed it to be a dispersed duplication: the polymorphism is actually located in the HLA region and is well tagged by HLA SNPs known to be associated with both diseases.

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010) also found that a novel HLA-region sequence insertion CNV (AC_000138.1_44) was associated with rheumatoid arthritis (p = 8.3 x 10(-4); OR = 0.87). The association replicated in 3,398 cases and 2,743 controls (replication p = 1.1 x 10(-3)).

subject: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010)
object: Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010) found no formally significant evidence replicating the reported association between CCL3L1 copy number and rheumatoid arthritis (nominal p = 0.058). None of the multiallelic CNVs they tested (CCL3L1, beta-defensins, FCGR3A/B) was significantly associated with the 3 autoimmune diseases after correction for multiple testing.

subject: Kochi et al. (2010)
object: Through a genome-wide association study of rheumatoid arthritis in Japanese individuals, Kochi et al. (2010) identified a polymorphism in CCR6 at 6q27, rs3093024, that was associated with RA susceptibility and was validated in 2 independent Japanese replication cohorts (a total of 7,069 cases and 20,727 controls; overall odds ratio = 1.19, P = 7.7 x 10(-19)).

object: Kochi et al. (2010) identified a triallelic dinucleotide polymorphism of CCR6 (CCR6DNP) in strong linkage disequilibrium with rs3093024 that showed effects on gene transcription. The CCR6DNP genotype correlated with CCR6 expression level and was associated with the presence of IL-17 in the sera of RA patients; the authors suggested that CCR6 is critically involved in IL-17-driven autoimmunity.
