subject: Stahl et al. (2010)
object: Stahl et al. (2010) performed a GWAS meta-analysis of 5,539 autoantibody-positive RA cases and 20,169 controls of European descent. They replicated the results in an independent set of 6,768 cases and 8,806 controls. Of 34 SNPs selected for replication, 10 reached genome-wide significance (P < 5 x 10(-8)) in the combined analysis of 41,282 samples. Seven of these were new RA risk loci, near genes including IL6ST, SPRED2, RBPJ, CCR6, IRF5, and PXK. With these loci, the number of confirmed RA risk loci in individuals of European ancestry rose to 31.

subject: Stahl et al. (2010)
object: Stahl et al. (2010) identified 3 RA risk loci that had not previously been implicated in RA or in any other autoimmune disease. The first was rs934734 at 2p14 (P overall = 5.3 x 10(-10)), within intron 1 of SPRED2. The second was rs6859219 at 5q11 (P overall = 9.6 x 10(-12)), in ANKRD55; the immunologic candidate IL6ST lies about 150 kb away, outside the region of LD. The third was rs26232 at 5q21 (P overall = 4.1 x 10(-8)), in an intron of the predicted gene C5orf30, where there was no obvious biologic candidate gene. Replication odds ratios for the minor alleles were 1.13, 0.85, and 0.93, respectively.

subject: Stahl et al. (2010)
object: Stahl et al. (2010) reported 11 more SNPs that replicated at P < 0.05 without reaching genome-wide significance. These included SNPs near IL6R, CD247, IL2/IL21, ZEB1, SH2B3, BATF, CD19/NFATC2IP, IKZF3, UBASH3A, and UBE2L3, many of them validated autoimmune risk alleles. Of 18 tested SNPs in LD with validated autoimmune risk alleles, 5 reached genome-wide significance and 7 showed suggestive association. The authors concluded that these results underscored the overlap between the genetic bases of RA and other autoimmune diseases.

subject: Stahl et al. (2010)
object: Stahl et al. (2010) noted that several of the associations, including those at RBPJ, CCR6, and CD247, further implicate T cells in RA pathogenesis. They also suggested that CCR6 could be a therapeutic target, because anti-CCR6 antibodies inhibit arthritis in mice.

subject: Stahl et al. (2010)
object: Stahl et al. (2010) estimated that the more than 30 validated non-MHC RA risk alleles explain 3.9% of total disease variance, of which 0.67% is due to the new alleles. Known genetic factors overall, including an estimated 12% for the MHC, explain only 16% of disease variance. In contrast, more than half the risk of autoantibody-positive RA is thought to be genetic.

subject: Kurreeman et al. (2011)
object: Kurreeman et al. (2011) used electronic health record (EHR) data linked to biospecimens to assemble a multi-ethnic case-control cohort of 1,515 rheumatoid arthritis cases and 1,480 controls, matched for genetic ancestry and anti-citrullinated protein antibody (ACPA) status. In individuals of European ancestry, the odds ratios and aggregate genetic risk score (GRS) of known RA risk alleles were nearly identical to those from a GWAS of 5,539 autoantibody-positive RA cases and 20,169 controls.

subject: Kurreeman et al. (2011)
object: Kurreeman et al. (2011) applied the same approach to other ethnic groups and found a large overlap in the genetic risk score for rheumatoid arthritis among individuals of European, African, East Asian, and Hispanic ancestry. They concluded that the genetic basis of RA risk is similar among cases of diverse ancestry.

subject: Kurreeman et al. (2011)
object: Kurreeman et al. (2011) found that the distribution of a genetic risk score based on 28 non-HLA rheumatoid arthritis risk alleles in ACPA-positive cases partially overlapped with that in the ACPA-negative subgroup of RA cases.

subject: Robinson et al. (2012)
object: Robinson et al. (2012) used a novel quantitative sequence variant assay together with an adapted paralogue ratio test to study copy number variants (CNVs) of FCGR3A and FCGR3B in 1,115 RA patients and 654 healthy volunteers. They analyzed the data with CNVtools, which accounts for batch effects and for uncertainty in copy number assignment. FCGR3B deletions were overrepresented in RA (OR 1.50, P = 0.028), and the association was stronger in rheumatoid factor-positive disease (OR 1.61, P = 0.011).

object: Robinson et al. (2012) found no association between RA and either duplications or deletions of FCGR3A.

subject: Robinson et al. (2012)
object: Robinson et al. (2012) showed that FcγRIIIb expression on neutrophils correlated with FCGR3B gene copy number. They suggested that neutrophils may play an important role in RA pathogenesis, possibly through reduced FcγRIIIb-mediated clearance of immune complexes.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: Okada et al. (2014) performed a three-stage trans-ethnic genome-wide association meta-analysis of rheumatoid arthritis in 29,880 cases and 73,758 controls of European and Asian ancestry, evaluating about 10 million SNPs. They identified 42 novel RA risk loci at genome-wide significance (P < 5.0 x 10(-8)), bringing the total number of RA risk loci to 101, including the MHC region.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: In Stage I, Okada et al. (2014) combined 22 GWAS of 19,234 cases and 61,565 controls and identified 57 loci at genome-wide significance, 17 of them novel. Loci with P < 5.0 x 10(-6) were then tested in Stage II (in silico) and Stage III (de novo) replication studies totaling 10,646 cases and 12,193 controls.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: The novel RA loci reported by Okada et al. (2014) included SNPs near TNFRSF9, IRF4, CDK6, ETS1, CD226, SYNGR1 (rs909685; trans-ethnic OR 1.13, P = 1.4 x 10(-16)), ATM, ILF3, IL20RB, and P2RY10 on the X chromosome.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: Across the 101 loci, Okada et al. (2014) found that risk allele frequencies and odds ratios were significantly correlated between Europeans and Asians, although 5 loci showed population-specific associations. The 100 non-MHC loci explained 5.5% of heritability in Europeans and 4.7% in Asians. The authors concluded that genetic risk of RA is largely shared between the two populations.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: Of 34 cell types tested, Okada et al. (2014) found that RA risk alleles were significantly enriched in H3K4me3 histone peaks only in primary CD4+ regulatory T cells. Pathway analysis showed enrichment for T-cell pathways, as well as B-cell and cytokine signaling pathways (IL-10, interferon, GM-CSF).

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: Genes at RA risk loci overlapped significantly with genes for primary immunodeficiency (14 of 194; strongest in the immune dysregulation category, with no overlap in innate immunity). They also overlapped with genes somatically mutated in hematologic cancers but not other cancers, and with knockout-mouse hematopoietic, immune, and cellular phenotypes. Okada et al. (2014) reported that about two-thirds of RA loci were shared with other traits, including vitiligo and primary biliary cirrhosis.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: Okada et al. (2014) scored the 377 genes at the 100 non-MHC loci against 8 criteria, including missense variants, cis-eQTL effects, protein-protein interactions, and mouse knockout phenotypes. They defined 98 genes as candidate biological RA risk genes, such as IL3 and CSF2 at 5q31. RA risk SNPs at 44 loci showed cis-eQTL effects, and 16% of risk SNPs were in linkage disequilibrium with missense SNPs.

subject: Okada et al. (2014)
object: Targets of approved RA drugs were significantly enriched, 3.7-fold, among the 98 biological RA risk genes and their protein-interaction partners. These targets included those of tocilizumab (IL6R), tofacitinib (JAK3), and abatacept (CTLA4-Ig). Okada et al. (2014) suggested that the cancer-drug targets CDK6 and CDK4 could be candidates for drug repurposing, noting that flavopiridol improves disease in animal models of RA.

subject: Raj et al. (2014)
object: Raj et al. (2014) did an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) study of purified naive CD4+ T cells and CD14+CD16- monocytes from 461 healthy individuals of European, African American, and East Asian ancestry. They found that susceptibility alleles for rheumatoid arthritis, as well as for multiple sclerosis and type 1 diabetes, were enriched for T cell-specific cis-regulatory effects. Susceptibility alleles for Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease were instead enriched for monocyte-specific effects. The authors concluded that this polarization implicates specific immune cell types in these diseases.

subject: Raj et al. (2014)
object: Raj et al. (2014) found that, of 425 GWAS SNPs associated with one or more autoimmune diseases, 143 had cis-regulatory effects on 164 genes in monocytes and/or T cells. This was a significant enrichment (permutation P < 1 x 10(-4)).

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) used BALB/c SKG mice, which develop T cell-mediated spontaneous autoimmune arthritis resembling RA due to a hypomorphic point mutation of ZAP-70, to isolate arthritogenic T cell receptors; among nine retrogenic strains each expressing a distinct TCR cloned from GFP- Valpha2+ Vbeta6+ CD4+ T cells of arthritic joints, those expressing the 7-39 or 6-39 TCR spontaneously developed arthritis at incidences of 80.0% and 27.3%, respectively, with mononuclear cell infiltration, pannus formation and cartilage destruction.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) reported that 66.7% of R7-39 retrogenic mice also developed chronic dermatitis exhibiting hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis, histopathological features of human psoriasis, whereas R6-39 mice did not; 7-39 TCR-transduced cells differentiated into monoclonal activated/memory CD4+ T cells that transferred both arthritis and dermatitis into other Rag2-/- mice, and the same TCR gene transferred into ZAP-70-intact BALB/c bone marrow did not cause arthritis because the T cells were largely negatively selected in the thymus or remained naive and anergic.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) identified by immunoblotting with sera from B cell-reconstituted R7-39 mice and mass spectrometry that the self-antigen recognized by the arthritogenic 7-39 TCR was the ubiquitously expressed 18-kD 60S ribosomal protein L23a (RPL23A), whose amino acid sequence is 100% conserved between mice and humans; recombinant RPL23A stimulated 7-39 hybridoma cells in a dose-dependent, MHC class II I-Ad-dependent manner, with the RPL23A71-90 peptide being the most potent stimulatory epitope.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) showed that CD4+ T cells, but not sera, from B cell-reconstituted R7-39 mice induced arthritis upon transfer into Rag2-/- mice, and that CD4+ T cells from arthritic joints or regional lymph nodes produced IL-17A, IFN-gamma and GM-CSF upon stimulation with RPL23A protein or the RPL23A71-90 peptide; regulatory T cells from BALB/c or SKG mice failed to suppress arthritis induced by activated or memory R7-39 TCR+ CD4+ T cells, although they effectively suppressed naive arthritogenic T cells.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) found by ELISA that serum anti-RPL23A IgG autoantibodies were present in a significantly higher proportion of rheumatoid arthritis patients (16.8% of 374) than in healthy controls (1.3% of 74); 2 of 23 psoriatic arthritis patients (8.7%) were positive, whereas none of 11 osteoarthritis, 30 systemic lupus erythematosus, or 10 polymyositis/dermatomyositis patients were positive.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) detected, in the synovial fluid of a subset of RA patients, CD4+ T cells that produced IFN-gamma upon stimulation with recombinant RPL23A (24 RA patients versus 9 healthy individuals tested), and demonstrated that RPL23A mRNA was ubiquitously expressed in healthy human tissues and that RPL23A protein was present in the cytoplasm of synovial cells, including CD55+ fibroblast-like synoviocytes, in both RA and osteoarthritis synovium; the authors suggested these responses may play a pathogenic role at least in a subset of patients with RA or psoriatic arthritis.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) noted that B cell-reconstituted R7-39 mice and arthritic SKG mice developed antibodies reacting with cyclic citrullinated peptides as observed in RA patients, but found no significant difference in anti-RPL23A antibody titer whether assessed with citrullinated or non-citrullinated RPL23A protein, and the stimulatory RPL23A71-90 peptide contained no arginine residue convertible to citrulline.

subject: Ito et al. (2014)
object: Ito et al. (2014) proposed that, since genetic polymorphism in a T cell signaling molecule is a major determinant of genetic susceptibility to human autoimmune diseases including RA, such genetic variation might at least in part alter thymic selection and thereby form a TCR repertoire capable of causing autoimmune disease.
